en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Twenty, Chapter on Mātaṅga.
13. The Hatthipāla Jātaka “After a long time indeed,
we behold this brahmin with the appearance of a god;”
With matted hair as thick as a load of hay,
with mud-stained teeth and dust on his head—
ah, after a long time indeed we see him!
The sage who delights in the qualities of the Dhamma,
clothed in saffron robes or covered with a garment of bark.
May your lordship accept from us a seat, water, and foot-wash;
we ask your lordship regarding the guest-offering.
“May your lordship show us honor.
“Seek wealth through the Vedas at will, dear son;
having established your sons and wife, [then come].”
“Having experienced all scents and tastes,
that sage who praises the forest is truly excellent.
“The Vedas are not the truth, nor is the acquisition of wealth;”
One does not overcome old age by obtaining a son;
the virtuous say that liberation lies in [renouncing] fragrances and flavors.
One’s rebirth into a state of fruition comes about through one’s own karma.
“Truly, this word of yours is the truth:
one’s rebirth and its fruit come about through one’s own karma.
And these parents of yours are now aged.”
“May they pass a hundred years free from disease.
“For whom death is a witness, O King,
and for whom old age is a friend, O best of men and heroes,” he said.
Even if one should know that one will never die,
and might see oneself healthy for a hundred years—
just as a man [might board] a boat upon the water...
If one tries to escape it, it nevertheless carries one to the shore;
even so, disease and constant old age carry the mortal into the power of the End-maker.
“Sensual pleasures are a mire, sensual pleasures are a swamp;
they are captivating, difficult to cross, the realm of death.
Sunk deep in this mire and swamp, [beings] are submerged.”
Those of inferior form do not cross to the further shore.
This one formerly committed cruel deeds;
he has been seized by me and shall certainly not be released.
"I will protect him with care;
let him not again perform such cruel deeds.
"Just as a man might search for a lost cow in the forest,"
The king searches, yet does not see him;
thus has my purpose, O King, been lost like an *esukārī* bird.
How then could I, O King, fail to search for it?
Day by day a person passes away,
and day by day they decline;
knowing that "the future does not exist," one should act accordingly.
What wise man would dispel a desire that has already arisen?
"I see this young maiden,
like one intoxicated, with eyes like *ketaka* flowers;"
While she has not yet enjoyed wealth and is still in her first youth,
Death seizes the maiden and departs.
Though he be young, well-born, fair-faced, and handsome—
Sāma, his beard covered with saffron powder, said:
“Having abandoned sensual pleasures and left home early, grant me permission, O Lord; I shall go forth.”
“A tree receives its designation by its branches;
but when its branches are stripped away, they call it a stump.
Today, O lady, my branches—my sons—have been stripped away.”
“Vāseṭṭhī, it is time for the alms-round.
“Like cranes in the sky when the snow has fallen,
the swans have burst through the nets they wove.”
"My sons and my husband are departing; how could I, understanding this, not follow them?
"These [pleasures], having been enjoyed and then vomited up,"
The birds are departing;
those who ate and then vomited have come into my hands.
The Brahmin has vomited up sensual pleasures;
you, O King, will vomit them back up again— like a man who eats what he has already vomited.
“He is not one to be praised.
Just as a strong man might lift up a weak man who has sunk and become mired in the mud, [so should one rescue another].
"Thus have you ferried me across,
O lady of Pañcāla, with well-spoken verses.
Having said this, the Great King—
Esukārī, lord of Disā,
having abandoned his kingdom, went forth like an elephant that has severed its bonds.
“The king, the best of heroic men,
having abandoned his kingdom, has set his heart on the going-forth;
may you also become just like the king.”
"Protected by us, please rule the kingdom.
But the king, that most excellent hero among men,
having renounced his realm, took delight in the life of renunciation.
I too shall wander alone in the world,
having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures;
even the king has taken delight in the going-forth.
Having abandoned the kingdom, the best of men and heroes,
I too shall wander alone in the world,
having renounced all sensual pleasures as they arise.
The nights pass away, their dark shadows fleeting;
the qualities of youth are gradually abandoned.
I too shall wander alone in this world.
Having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures,
time passes and nights elapse;
the qualities of youth gradually fade away.
I too shall wander alone in the world, having abandoned all sensual desires as they arise.
Time passes; the nights hasten by.
The qualities of age fade away in succession;
I too shall wander alone in the world,
having become cool and transcended all attachment.
The Thirteenth Birth Story: Hatthipāla Jātaka.
